turns.question: How does a B-tree organize data on disk?
turns.answer: A B-tree breaks the database into fixed-size pages and overwrites a page in place when its contents change.

message: Why does it write each piece of data to disk more than once?
standalone: Why does a B-tree write each piece of data to disk more than once?
key_facts: A B-tree writes every piece of data at least twice: once to the write-ahead log and once to the tree page itself

turns.question: What can go wrong when a client holding a lock lease pauses for a long time?
turns.answer: The lease can expire during the pause, so another client may take the lock while the first client still writes to storage as if it held it.

turns.question: How does a leader detect that a follower has failed?
turns.answer: It uses a timeout: a follower that does not respond within the timeout is declared dead.

message: Back to the first problem: how can the system guard against that one?
standalone: A client holds a lock, pauses for a long time, then writes to storage after its lock has expired. How can the storage service protect itself from that stale write?
key_facts: The lock service returns a fencing token, a number that increases every time a lock is granted
The storage service rejects a write carrying a token older than one it has already processed
notes: converted from the Phase 3 draft; executor draft, owner must review

turns.question: How does two-phase commit decide whether to commit a distributed transaction?
turns.answer: The coordinator asks every participant to prepare, and commits only if all of them vote yes.

message: Why do log-structured storage engines use probabilistic set membership structures for key lookups?
standalone: Why do log-structured storage engines use probabilistic set membership structures for key lookups?
key_facts: Looking up a key that does not exist is slow because the memtable and all segments back to the oldest must be checked
A Bloom filter is a memory-efficient structure approximating a set, and it can tell that a key does not exist, saving disk reads
notes: converted from the Phase 3 draft; executor draft, owner must review

turns.question: What is column-oriented storage?
turns.answer: Column-oriented storage keeps all the values of each column together instead of keeping all the values of each row together.

message: How can a system prevent a user from seeing time appear to go backward when making successive read queries against asynchronous replicas?
standalone: How can a system prevent a user from seeing time appear to go backward when making successive read queries against asynchronous replicas?
key_facts: Each user's read requests should always go to the same replica
evidence_terms: makes their reads from the same replica
notes: converted from the Phase 3 draft; executor draft, owner must review

turns.question: How do leader-based and leaderless replication differ in where writes go?
turns.answer: In leader-based replication every write goes to one leader that forwards it to followers; in leaderless replication the client sends each write to several replicas directly.

turns.question: How do LSM-trees and B-trees store data differently?
turns.answer: LSM-trees write sorted segment files and merge them in the background, while B-trees update fixed-size pages in place.

turns.question: What is a dirty read in a transaction?
turns.answer: A dirty read happens when a transaction sees data that another transaction has written but not yet committed.

message: How do transaction processing systems typically enforce that concurrent updates to the same database object do not overwrite uncommitted changes?
standalone: How do transaction processing systems typically enforce that concurrent updates to the same database object do not overwrite uncommitted changes?
key_facts: Databases prevent dirty writes using row-level locks
A transaction must acquire the lock on an object before modifying it
evidence_terms: prevent dirty writes by using row-level locks
notes: converted from the Phase 3 draft; executor draft, owner must review

turns.question: What does eventual consistency guarantee for replicas?
turns.answer: If writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value, but a read may return a stale value in the meantime.

message: What is the key timing property that distinguishes linearizability from eventual consistency?
standalone: What is the key timing property that distinguishes linearizability from eventual consistency?
key_facts: Linearizability is a recency guarantee: a read returns the most recent, up-to-date value
notes: converted from the Phase 3 draft; executor draft, owner must review

turns.question: What is a quorum in leaderless replication?
turns.answer: With n replicas, every write must be confirmed by w nodes and every read must query r nodes; choosing w + r > n lets a read see the latest write.

message: What if it accepts writes on other nodes during a network outage?
standalone: What happens when a leaderless database accepts writes on reachable nodes outside a key's designated home nodes during a network outage?
key_facts: It is a sloppy quorum: writes are accepted on reachable nodes outside the key's designated home nodes
Hinted handoff later sends those writes to the home nodes once the interruption is fixed
notes: executor draft from q021; owner must review

turns.question: What is a hot spot when partitioning data?
turns.answer: A hot spot is a partition with disproportionately high load, for example when many reads and writes go to the same key.

message: How can the application spread the writes for that one key?
standalone: What application-level modification can distribute write requests across multiple partitions when a single key receives an extreme volume of concurrent updates?
key_facts: Reduce skew by adding a random number to the beginning or end of the hot key
evidence_terms: add a random number to the beginning or end of the key
notes: executor draft from q027; owner must review

turns.question: What is read repair?
turns.answer: When a client reads from several replicas and sees a stale value on one of them, it writes the newer value back to that replica.

message: Why is relying only on that risky for records that are rarely read?
standalone: Why do leaderless replication systems that rely exclusively on client-side fixes during query execution risk reduced durability for infrequently accessed records?
key_facts: Without an anti-entropy process, rarely read values can be missing from some replicas, because read repair only happens when a value is read
evidence_terms: read repair is only performed when a value is read
notes: executor draft from q031; owner must review

turns.question: What is two-phase locking?
turns.answer: A transaction acquires locks and holds them until it commits, so writers block readers and readers block writers.

turns.question: What is serializable snapshot isolation?
turns.answer: Transactions proceed without blocking, and at commit time the database checks for conflicts and aborts a transaction whose premise became outdated.

message: How do these two approaches differ in handling conflicts?
standalone: How do pessimistic concurrency control mechanisms and optimistic concurrency control mechanisms differ in their handling of conflicting transaction operations?
key_facts: Pessimistic concurrency control blocks by holding locks
Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions run without blocking and aborts at commit if a conflict is detected
notes: executor draft from q034; owner must review

turns.question: How does a B-tree store data?
turns.answer: A B-tree breaks the database into fixed-size pages and overwrites a page in place when it changes.

turns.question: What is an LSM-tree?
turns.answer: A log-structured merge-tree writes sorted segment files and merges and compacts them in the background.

message: Which of the two is faster for writes, and which for reads?
standalone: What are the trade-offs between LSM-trees and B-trees regarding write throughput versus read throughput?
key_facts: LSM-trees are typically faster for writes, while B-trees are thought to be faster for reads
Reads are slower on LSM-trees because they must check several data structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction
evidence_terms: LSM-trees are typically faster for writes
notes: executor draft from q022; owner must review

turns.question: What are the two ways to partition a secondary index?
turns.answer: By document, where each partition indexes only its own documents, or by term, where all index entries for a term live on one partition.

message: How do the two compare when you query them?
standalone: How do document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes compare to term-partitioned (global) secondary indexes?
key_facts: Document-partitioned indexes keep a separate index in each partition, so a read must query all partitions (scatter/gather)
Term-partitioned indexes let a read go to a single partition, but writes are slower and more complicated
notes: executor draft from q023; owner must review

turns.question: What is an SSTable?
turns.answer: A Sorted String Table is a segment file whose key-value pairs are sorted by key, with each key appearing only once in the file.

message: Why does that mean it does not need every key in memory?
standalone: A storage engine keeps its data files sorted by key. How does that let it find a key without holding every key in memory?
key_facts: The in-memory index can be sparse, holding one key for every few kilobytes of the sorted segment file
That is enough because a few kilobytes can be scanned quickly
evidence_terms: one key for every few kilobytes
notes: executor draft from q014; owner must review

turns.question: What does a stream processor do?
turns.answer: It consumes event streams and processes each event as it arrives, for example to update a derived dataset.

turns.question: What kinds of joins do stream processors perform?
turns.answer: Stream-stream joins, stream-table joins and table-table joins.

message: How do the first two of those differ in operation?
standalone: What is the operational difference between a stream-stream join and a stream-table join?
key_facts: A stream-stream (window) join matches events from two streams within a time window
A stream-table join enriches stream events by looking up records in a table that is kept up to date
notes: executor draft from q025; owner must review

turns.question: How does a leader replicate writes to followers?
turns.answer: The leader writes each change to its replication log and sends it to every follower, which applies the changes in the same order.

message: What is the difference between checking data structure when reading versus checking structure when writing in document stores?
standalone: What is the difference between checking data structure when reading versus checking structure when writing in document stores?
key_facts: Schema-on-read means the structure of the data is implicit and only interpreted when it is read
Schema-on-write means the schema is explicit and the database ensures written data conforms to it
notes: executor draft from q018; owner must review

turns.question: What is write skew?
turns.answer: Two transactions read the same objects and then each updates a different object based on what it read, so together they break an invariant.

message: How can an application be built by composing specialized storage and processing systems around dataflow, instead of relying on one monolithic database?
standalone: How can an application be built by composing specialized storage and processing systems around dataflow, instead of relying on one monolithic database?
key_facts: The idea is unbundling databases: composing specialized storage and processing systems with application code, also called the database inside-out approach
notes: executor draft from q020; owner must review

turns.question: What is a secondary index?
turns.answer: An additional index on a field other than the primary key, so records can be found by the value of that field.

message: How do immutable append-only logs protect applications from permanent data corruption when faulty or incorrect code is deployed?
standalone: How do immutable append-only logs protect applications from permanent data corruption when faulty or incorrect code is deployed?
key_facts: Because immutable logs avoid destructive overwrites, buggy code cannot permanently corrupt the original input data
Operators can fix the code and rerun the processing over the untouched data
notes: executor draft from q037; owner must review

turns.question: How does a leaderless database recover a node that was down?
turns.answer: When the node comes back, read repair and an anti-entropy process copy the writes it missed from the other replicas.

message: How do query engines minimize CPU branch mispredictions and function call overhead when processing filtering conditions over columnar storage?
standalone: How do query engines minimize CPU branch mispredictions and function call overhead when processing filtering conditions over columnar storage?
key_facts: Vectorized processing iterates over chunks of column data in a tight loop
This avoids function calls and branch mispredictions for each record
notes: executor draft from q040; owner must review

turns.question: How does Twitter deliver tweets to home timelines?
turns.answer: One approach looks up the users someone follows and merges their tweets when the timeline is read; another inserts each new tweet into every follower's timeline cache.

message: Why does Twitter use a hybrid approach combining write fan-out and read-side merging for user timelines?
standalone: Why does Twitter use a hybrid approach combining write fan-out and read-side merging for user timelines?
key_facts: For most users, tweets are fanned out into followers' home timeline caches when they are posted
Tweets from celebrities with very many followers are fetched when the timeline is read and merged in, instead of being fanned out

turns.question: What is a Byzantine fault?
turns.answer: A node behaves arbitrarily, for example by sending corrupted or deliberately misleading messages to other nodes.

message: What foundational assumption do most non-cryptographic distributed database algorithms make regarding the integrity of messages received from participating cluster nodes?
standalone: What foundational assumption do most non-cryptographic distributed database algorithms make regarding the integrity of messages received from participating cluster nodes?
key_facts: Algorithms assume nodes are unreliable but honest: they may be slow or crash, but any message they send follows the protocol rules and is not malicious or corrupted
notes: executor draft from q030; owner must review

turns.question: What is Avro?
turns.answer: A binary encoding format that started in Hadoop; data is encoded with a schema and the encoded bytes contain no field tags.

message: How do binary serialization formats designed for big data file processing allow reading systems to parse historical records generated under older schemas without requiring code modifications or data re-encoding?
standalone: How do binary serialization formats designed for big data file processing allow reading systems to parse historical records generated under older schemas without requiring code modifications or data re-encoding?
key_facts: Avro compares the writer's schema (stored with the data) with the reader's schema (in the application)
It translates the data from the writer's schema into the reader's schema when decoding

turns.question: How can a batch job count how often each page was viewed?
turns.answer: It can keep a hash table of counters in memory, or sort the records by page and count adjacent records.

message: Why does sorting records scale better to datasets exceeding available system RAM than accumulating occurrence counts in memory data structures?

Sorting can spill to disk and uses sequential disk I/O

turns.question: What is a distributed transaction?
turns.answer: A transaction that writes to several nodes and must either commit on all of them or abort on all of them.

message: 2PC vs 3PC

key_facts: 2PC guarantees atomic commit but is blocking: it can get stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover
3PC is a proposed nonblocking alternative that assumes bounded network delay and bounded response times

turns.question: What is a property graph?
turns.answer: A graph in which every vertex and every edge has a label and a set of key-value properties.

turns.answer: A document-partitioned index keeps each partition's index local to its documents; a term-partitioned index is global and split across partitions by term.

turns.answer: JSON does not distinguish integers from floating-point numbers, and it does not specify a precision.

turns.question: How do distributed systems detect a node that has failed?
turns.answer: Usually with a timeout: if a node does not respond within some time, it is declared dead.
